title: Lewis Hamilton says there is ‘much still to do’ on improving diversity in F1 after Mission 44 report
content:
Lewis Hamilton says Formula 1 has “much still to do” on improving diversity at teams competing in the championship, with his comments made in a new report from his charity initiative, Mission 44.

Hamilton founded Mission 44 in 2021, a year after he initiated the Hamilton Commission, with the United Kingdom’s Royal Academy of engineering, to assess underrepresentation of Black people in motorsport.

Ahead of the fifth anniversary of Mission 44’s founding, it has released a report titled “Igniting Inclusion” that charts the progress on key 10 recommendations in the Hamilton Commission’s 2021 report, “Accelerating Change: Improving Representation of Black People in UK Motorsport.”

The 10 steps were outlined for UK motorsport organizations — including F1 teams — and education centers.

Igniting Inclusion “audits what has been done against those 10 recommendations, examines what the sport can and cannot show about its workforce today, and proposes three new recommendations for 2026 to 2031,” per the report’s introduction.

The report finds that while improvements have been made since 2021, it concludes F1 overall lacks data to “show whether these efforts have changed who enters, progresses and stays in motorsport.”

It now recommends three changes to be implemented over the next five years, with a particular focus on the constraints posed by F1’s cost cap when it comes to careers development.

The report also widens the remit on recommendations to include data on women and younger people from lower socio-economic backgrounds and their representation in motorsport organizations.

In the report’s opening remarks, Hamilton said: “When I walk through the (F1) paddock now, I see more women, more Black and Brown faces, more people who look like the fans in the grandstands than at any point since I started. That is heartening, and the people behind it deserve credit.

“And yet, there is much still to do. We have opened the door, but we have not yet learned to count how many people walk through it, or how many stay.”

The report’s three recommendations are for all 11 F1 teams, the F1 organization and the FIA — the governing body for world motorsport — to report staff numbers, promotions and exits “by gender, ethnicity and socio-economic background.” All F1 teams are called on to provide dedicated early-career places and support and publish the numbers around these.

The report also calls for a dedicated category of talent investment” to be “excluded from the cost cap, starting with new apprentice salaries” and for the teams, F1 organization and the FIA to invest a minimum of $66 million for assisting young people “from underrepresented backgrounds into motorsport careers, and supporting them to stay.”

F1’s cost cap restricts team spending each year, with the 2026 figure set at $215 million.

While it has been credited with massively inflating team worth and creating a new degree of financial stability across the teams compared to previous eras, its constraints have led to a squeeze on staff salaries, particularly at the lowest levels.

The three highest staff salaries at each team, meanwhile, are excluded. As are driver salaries and the costs for several other team departments. Mercedes team boss Toto Wolff recently told Sky Sports F1 that team junior staff salaries are “suppressed” as a result of the cost cap.

“Measure who joins, who is promoted and who stays, and let the best practice be recognized,” Hamilton said about the recommendations. “Take investment in people out of the cost cap and put money behind the pipeline together.

“Fix the front door and publish the paid places you will offer every year. None of it is beyond a sport that already knows how to measure, improve and be ambitious.”

The Igniting Inclusion report comes just a month after the F1 organization released its first Social Impact report.

This committed the F1 organization to improving its measurement of the sport’s social impact. It also said its next steps on improving diversity in F1 a had a “focus on young people and underrepresented communities.”

In a joint statement supplied to The Athletic, the F1 organization and the FIA said: “We are proud of the programs and initiatives which help inspire the next generation of Formula 1 and how they continue to increase access and opportunity across our sport.

“Following recommendations from the Hamilton Commission, the sport signed its first ever D&I charter in 2024, and in 2025 conducted its first ever sport wide data gathering exercise to capture the global reach of our social impact programs.

“This showed that in 2025 season alone, more than 500,000 young people engaged in education, STEM and inspiration programs globally and over 1000 structured skills and talent development opportunities across our sport.

“As F1 continues to grow on the global stage, so too does our ambition to deepen and evolve our social impact. We are committed, alongside the F1 teams, the FIA and broader members of our sport to continue build on this foundation and look forward to sharing the next phase of our work.”
